item.title: 11 Introduction
item.description:
[[P552]]SECTION IV

CHAPTER XI

[[TIRTHAYĀTRĀ|TĪRTHAYĀTRĀ]] (pilgrimages to holy places)

All religions have laid great emphasis on the sacredness of certain localities and have either enjoined or recommended with great insistence pilgrimages to them. Among the five incumbent practical religious duties1 of a Moslem, pilgrimage at least once in his life to Mecca and Medina, the birth place and burial place of the prophet Mohammad, is one. The four places of pilgrimage for Buddhists have been the place of the birth of Buddha ([[Lumbini|Lumbinī]] or Rummindei), the place where he attained perfect enlightenment (Bodh Gayā), the place where he set in motion the wheel of dharma by delivering his first sermon (at Sārnāth near [[Benares )|Benares)]] and the place where he passed away into the state of [[nirvana|nirvāṇa]] (Kusinārā). Vide Mahāparinibbānasutta (S. B. E. vol. XI. p. 90). For Christians Jerusalem has been the holiest place and no religious [[com munity|community]] except the Christians undertook in historic times several great military pilgrimages. The crusades were launched to free the Holy Land of Christians from the domination of Moslems. In spite of what Gibbon says2 somewhat cynically about those who joined the crusades, it must be admitted that there were thousands among the crusaders who risked their lives and fortunes in the pursuit of an ideal. In India holy places have played a very important part. Large rivers, mountains and forests have always been venerated as sacred3 [[P553]]and as the abodes of gods. In ancient and medieval India pilgrimages brought many advantages to the community as well as to the pilgrims themselves. Though India was divided into many kingdoms and the people of India followed several cults and sub-cults, pilgrimages tended to foster the idea of the essential and fundamental unity of Indian culture and of India [[also,|also.]] Benares and Rāmeśvara were held sacred by all Hindus, whether they hailed from the north of India or from the peninsula. Though the Hindu community was broken up into numerous castes and suffered from caste exclusiveness, [[pilgrim ages|pilgrimages]] tended to level up all men by bringing them together to the same holy rivers or shrines. The traditions associated with holy places, the discipline through which the pilgrims passed, association with holy and philosophic men and the whole [[atmos phere|atmosphere]] and environment at [[tirthas|tīrthas]] made it easy for pilgrims to remain at a high spiritual level and inculcated in them a mood of reverence that lasted long even after they returned from the [[pilgrimage,|pilgrimage.]] Pilgrimages supplied the much needed stimulus to draw ordinary men away from selfish pursuits and to make them think of the higher and more enduring moral and spiritual values. These obvious benefits and the belief that a holy place was the abode of some divinity led ancient dharmaśāstra writers to lay emphasis on visits to [[tirthas.|tīrthas.]] The [[Visṇu|Viṣṇu]] Dh. S. provides4 that the dharma common to all men comprises the following: forbearance, truthfulness, restraint of the mind, cleanliness, charity, control of the senses, [[ahimsā,|ahiṁsā,]] obedience to elders, visiting holy places, compassion, straightforwardness, [[P554]]freedom from avarice, honouring gods and [[brāhmanas|brāhmaṇas]] and freedom from jealousy. Modern men whose faith in some of the aspects of the religious beliefs of our forefathers has been weakened or altogether sapped by the sight of the professional ministrants at the [[tirthas|tīrthas]] and their rapacity and ignorance should not judge the ancient attitude towards [[tirthas|tīrthas]] harshly.

item.title: 12 The Ganges
item.description:
[[P585]]CHAPTER XII

THE GANGES

Since the Ganges is the holiest of rivers and since such highly esteemed [[tirthas|tīrthas]] as Kanakhala, Haridvāra, Prayāga and Kāśi are situated on it, it would be most proper to begin the treatment of individual [[tirthas|tīrthas]] with the Ganges.

[[1. It|It]] has been already seen (p. 556) how the Ganges is the first among the many rivers invoked in the famous [[Nadāstuti|Nadīstuti]] hymn ([[Rg.|Ṛg.]] X. 75. 5-6). In [[Rg.1323|Ṛg.]]1 VI. 45. 31 we have the word ‘[[Gāngyah’|Gāṅgyaḥ’]] which most probably means ‘growing on the Ganges’. In the [[Satapatha Brāhmana|Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa]] XIII. 5. 4. 11 and 13 and Ait. Br. 39. 9 the victories and sacrifices of Bharata [[Daussanti|Dauṣṣanti]] on the [[Ganga|Gaṅgā]] and Yamunā are mentioned. In [[Sat. Br.|Śat. Br.]] XIII. 5. 4. 11 and 13 an ancient [[gātha|gāthā]] is quoted ‘At [[Nadapit|Nāḍapit]] the Apsaras [[Sakuntala|Śakuntalā]] conceived Bharata who after conquering the whole earth brought to Indra more than 1000 horses meet for sacrifice.’ The Mahābhārata (Anuśāsana 26. 26-103) and the Purāṇas (such as [[Nāradiya,|Nāradīya,]] Uttarārdha, chap. 38-45 and 51. 1-48, Padma V. 60. 1-127, Agni chap. 110, Matsya chap. 180-185, Padma, [[Adikhanda.|Ādikhaṇḍa,]] chap. 33-37) contain hundreds of verses eulogising the greatness and the sanctifying activity of the Ganges. The Skandapurāṇa, [[Kāśikhanda,|Kāśīkhaṇḍa,]] chap. 29 (verses 17-168) contains one thousand names of the Ganges. It is not possible to reproduce here even a small fraction of what is said in these works about the Ganges. To most men in India great rivers like the Ganges, great mountains like the Himālaya present a double aspect, [[viz,|viz.]] the physical aspect and the spiritual aspect. A great river apart from its volume of water is deemed to have a [[spiri tual|spiritual]] or divine life which animates it. Tylor (in ‘Primitive Culture’, 2nd [[ed.p|ed. p.]] 477) observes ‘What we call inanimate objects—rivers, stones, trees, weapons and so forth—are treated as living intelligent beings, talked to, propitiated, punished for the harm they do.’ There are separate treatises devoted to the [[glorifica tion|glorification]] of the Ganges and the pilgrimage to it such as the [[P586]][[Gangāpattalaka|Gaṅgāpattalaka]] of Gaṇeśvara (1350 A. D.), [[Gangāvākyāvali|Gaṅgāvākyāvalī]] of [[Viśvāsadevi,|Viśvāsadevī,]] queen of king [[Padmasimha|Padmasiṃha]] of Mithilā, the [[Gangābhakti-tarangiṇi|Gaṅgābhakti-taraṅgiṇī]] of [[Ganapati,|Gaṇapati,]] the [[Gangākrtyaviveka|Gaṅgākṛtyaviveka]] of Vardhamāna. Vide [[H, of Dh,|H. of Dh.]] vol. I. p. 538 for the dates of some of these works.

item.title: 13 Kāśī
item.description:
[[P618]]CHAPTER XIII

[[KAŚĪ|KĀŚĪ]]

There is hardly any city in the world that can claim greater antiquity, greater continuity and greater popular veneration than Banaras. Banaras has been a holy city for at least thirty centuries. No city in India arouses the religious emotions of Hindus as much as [[Kāśi|Kāśī]] does. To the Hindu mind it represents great and unbroken traditions of religious sanctity and learning. It is a miniature of Hindu life through the ages in all its great complexities and contradictions. Not only Hinduism with its numerous sects has flourished here for numberless centuries, but the principles of Buddhism, one of the great religions of the world, were first proclaimed here by [[Sākyamuni|Śākyamuni]] after he received Enlightenment at Bodh-Gayā under the Bodhi tree. Thousands of verses are found in the epics and purāṇas about Banaras. Several volumes have been written about Banares during the last hundred years.1 It would be impossible to do justice here to this vast mass of literature on Banaras. I shall briefly deal with the important topics relating to Banaras. In olden times the name was spelt as Benares, but recently as Banaras, which will be retained here (except in quotations).

item.title: 14 Gayā
item.description:
[[P643]]CHAPTER XIV

[[GAYA|GAYĀ]]

Gayā occupies a unique place in the hearts of all pious Hindus even in these days. Hundreds of pages have been written about the history, the antiquities, the architectural remains of Gayā, the sacred places in and round about Gayā, the śrāddha rites performed in Gayā and about Gayāwals (the priests of Gayā). It is not possible to deal with this vast mass in this work. But it is impossible not to say a few words about the many conflicting views on certain important matters put forward by scholars for about three quarters of a century. Those who are deeply interested in the history and antiquities of [[Gaya|Gayā]] should carefully read the following books and papers; Dr. Rajendralal Mitra’s [[‘Buddha-Gaya’|‘Buddha-Gayā’]] with 51 plates (1878); General Cunningham’s ‘Mahābodhi’ with 31 plates at the end (1892); L. [[S.S.|S. S.]] O’Malley’s District Gazetteer of Gayā, vol. XII and J. [[A.S.B.|A. S. B.]] for 1903 LXXII, No. 3, pp. 1-11 on [[‘Gayāśrāddha and Gayāvals;’|‘Gayāśrāddha and Gayāwals;’]] Indian Antiquary, vol. X pp. 339-340 for a Chinese Inscription at Buddha Gayā dated in a Chinese date corresponding to 1033 [[A, D,|A. D.]] and pp. 341-347 for Inscriptions at Gayā, one of which is engraved in a temple of the Sun near a tank [[‘Daksinamānasa’|‘Dakṣiṇamānasa’]] near the [[Visnupada,|Viṣṇupada,]] dated 1813 years after Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa; Indian Antiquary, vol. 16 pp. 63 ff Inscription of Yakṣapāla, son of Viśvāditya, which records the building of a temple for certain images in the 15th regnal year of the Pāla king Nayapāladeva who died in 1045 [[A, D.,|A. D.,]] edited by Kielhorn; Dr. Benimadhav Barua’s [[‘Gayā and Buddha Gayā’|‘Gayā and Buddha-Gayā’]] in two volumes (1934) with plates; Journal of Bihar and Orissa R. Society, vol. 24 (for 1938) pp. 89-111 where [[Dr.J.C.|Dr. J. C.]] Ghose deals with ’the antiquity of Gayā.’ Some of the remarks of Dr. Ghose are most unwarranted and cannot be accepted, such as holding ‘maganda’ in ‘Pramagandasya’ in [[Rg.|Ṛg.]] III. [[53.14|53. 14]] as identical with Magadha and the explanation of [[‘udantyāh’in|‘udantyāḥ’ in]] the Ait. Br. as ‘people of sunrise.’ Among medieval digests Gayā is dealt with in Kalpataru on [[Tirthas|Tīrthas]] pp. 163-174, [[Tyrblade cintāmani|Tīrtha-cintāmaṇi]] of Vācaspati pp. 268-328, Tristhalīsetu of [[Narayana ) bhatta|Nārāyaṇa-bhaṭṭa]] pp. 316-379, [[Tirthaprakāśa|Tīrthaprakāśa]] pp. 384-452, [[Tirthendi, sekhara|Tīrthendu-śekhara]] pp. 54–59, [[Triṣthalisetu-sāra-sangraha|Triṣthalīsetu-sāra-saṅgraha]] of [[Bhattojin|Bhaṭṭoji]] pp. 36-38.

item.title: 15 Kurukṣetra and Other Famous Tīrthas
item.description:
[[P680]]CHAPTER XV

[[KURUKSETRA|KURUKṢETRA]] AND SOME OTHER FAMOUS

TĪRTHAS

[[KURUKSETRA|KURUKṢETRA]] (25 miles east of Ambala) is a very sacred tract, the history of which is lost in the mists of [[anti quity.|antiquity.]] In the [[Rgveda X, 33.4|Ṛgveda X. 33. 4]] there is a reference to a king [[Kurusravana,|Kuruśravaṇa,]] son of [[Trasadasyu,1538|Trasadasyu]]1 The [[Atharva-veda men tions|Atharva-veda mentions]] a Kauravya husband (probably a king) who had a talk with his wife.2 In the times of the Brāhmaṇas [[Kuruksetra|Kurukṣetra]] had become a very holy land. The [[Sat. Br. (IV.1.5.13)|Śat. Br. (IV. 1. 5. 13)]] narrates the legend that the gods performed a sacrifice in [[Kuruksetra|Kurukṣetra]] and at first excluded the two [[Asvins|Aśvins]] from any share in it (S. B. E. vol. 26 p. 275). The [[Maitrāyani Samhitā|Maitrāyaṇī Saṁhitā]] (II. 1. 4., devā vai sattramāsata [[Kuruksetre)|Kurukṣetre)]] and the [[Tai. Br. (V.1.1.,|Tai. Br. (V. 1. 1.,]] devā vai sattram-āsata [[teṣām Kuruksetram vedir-āsit)|teṣāṁ Kurukṣetraṁ vedir-āsīt)]] also say that the Gods performed a [[satira|sattra]] in [[Kuruksetra.|Kurukṣetra.]] The idea underlying these passages appears to be this. The Vedic people of the [[Brāhmana|Brāhmaṇa]] period held yajñas to be the dharma par excellence, as stated in [[Rg. X. 90.16|Ṛg. X. 90. 16]] (yajñena yajñam-ayajanta [[devāstāni dharmāni prathamānyāsan).|devāstāni dharmāṇi prathamānyāsan).]] [[Kuruksetra|Kurukṣetra]] was the centre of [[✓ Vedic|Vedic]] culture in the [[Brāhmana|Brāhmaṇa]] period and sacrifices must have been performed there on a large scale. Hence it was called [[dharmaksetra|dharmakṣetra]] and as gods were supposed to have attained their position by what men believed to be dharma (yajña, tapas &c.) it is stated that gods performed sattras in [[Kuruksetra.|Kurukṣetra.]] The same Brāhmaṇa mentions a Kauravya king [[Bahlika Prātipiya (XII. 9.3.3, S. B, E.|Bahlika Prātipīya (XII. 9. 3. 3, S. B. E.]] vol. 44 p. 269). The [[Tai. Br. (1. 8.4.1)|Tai. Br. (I. 8. 4. 1)]] informs us that the Kuru-Pañcālas went towards the east in winter [[(śiśıra)|(śiśira)]] and to the west in summer which was the worst season. The references in the Ait. Br. are far more instructive. The legend about Kavaṣa in which [[Sarasvati|Sarasvatī]] helps the sage has already been referred to above (p. 559 n. 1254). [[The Ait Br (8.1 or II 19) calls that place, where Sarasvati came rushing. Parisaraka’.|The Ait. Br. (8. 1 or II 19) calls that place, where Sarasvatī came rushing, ‘Pariśaraka’.]] In another place the Ait. Br. tells us that in its time Nyagrodha (Ficus India) was called Nyubja in [[Kuru A|Kuru]][[P681]]kṣetra.3 Elsewhere the Ait. Br. speaks of the countries of the Kurus and [[Pancalas|Pañcālas]] together with the [[Vasa-Usinaras|Vaśa-Uśīnaras]] (38. [[3=VIII.|3 = VIII.]] 14). [[The Tai. Ā, narrates 1541|The Tai. Ā. narrates]]4 that the gods performed a sattra and [[Kuruksetra|Kurukṣetra]] was their altar (for the sattra). The southern side of that Vedi (i. e. [[Kuruksetra)|Kurukṣetra)]] was [[Khāndava,|Khāṇḍava,]] the northern side was Tūrghna, the hinder part was [[Parīpah,|Pariṇah,]] and the country of Maru (desert) was the [[rubbisn|rubbish]] pit. This shows that [[Khāndava,|Khāṇḍava,]] Tūrghna and [[Parinah|Pariṇah]] were border parts of [[Kuruksetra|Kurukṣetra]] and the Maru district was somewhat away from [[Kuruksetra.|Kurukṣetra.]] The [[Srautasūtras|Śrautasūtras]] of [[Āśv. XII, 6, Lātyāyana X. 15 ft. and Katyāyana 1542 24.6.5 ff|Āśv. XII. 6, Lāṭyāyana X. 15 ff. and Kātyāyana]]5 24. 6. 5 ff closely follow [[Tāndya|Tāṇḍya]] and other Brāhmaṇas and mention several holy places at which parts of the Sārasvata sattras were performed such as [[Plaksa Prasravana|Plakṣa Prasravaṇa]] where [[Sarasvati|Sarasvatī]] starts, the Vaitandhava-hrada of [[Sarasvati,|Sarasvatī,]] the tract called [[Parinah in Kuruksetra,|Pariṇah in Kurukṣetra,]] Yamunā flowing through the country of Kārapacava and the country of [[Triplaksāvaharana,|Triplakṣāvaharaṇa.]]

item.title: 16 List of Tīrthas
item.description:
[[P723]]CHAPTER XVI

[[LIST OF TĪRTHÁS|LIST OF TĪRTHAS]]

This is merely a list of [[tirthas|tīrthas]] from the point of view of Dharmaśāstra and not a treatise on the Ancient Geography of India. The result is that many countries and towns that have no importance or claims as [[tirthas|tīrthas]] have been altogether omitted. Bauddha and Jain works on [[tirthas|tīrthas]] have only rarely been referred to. Many of the [[Purānas|Purāṇas]] enumerate the [[moun tains|mountains]] and rivers of [[dvipas|dvīpas]] and [[var ṣas|varṣas]] other than those of [[Jambudvipa|Jambudvīpa]] and [[Bhārata-varsa|Bhārata-varṣa]] such as Harivarṣa, [[Ramyaka varsa|Ramyaka-varṣa]], [[Krauñcadvipa|Krauñcadvīpa]], [[Sālmalidvipa|Śālmalidvīpa]], but they have been [[exclud ed|excluded]] from this list. The Brahmapurāṇa (chap. 26 verses 8-83) contains a string of over 520 [[tirthas|tīrthas]] without hardly any certain indication of their location and the Bhīṣmaparva in chap. 9 mentions about 160 rivers with practically no indication about their location in most cases. Similarly, the [[Garuda|Garuḍa]] (I. 81. 1-31) enumerates about 200 and Padma (VI. 129) contains 108 [[tirtha|tīrtha]] names. In Banaras alone I have listed about 350 [[sub tirthas|sub-tīrthas]]. But there are about 1500 shrines and temples in Banaras alone. These have not been included. Each great [[tirtha|tīrtha]] has numerous sub-tīrthas as in the Varāha-purāṇa under Mathurā, in Brahma-purāṇa under [[Gautami|Gautamī]], in Vāyu-purāṇa under [[Gaya|Gayā]]. Through sheer weariness or inadvertence some of these must have been left out by me and some were left out purposely on account of the absence of any importance. Besides, several [[tirthas|tīrthas]] that are regarded as sacred by modern people are not so treated in the Epics or purāṇas and are not even mentioned in them; many of these have been omitted in this list. Our authorities are often very vague about the location or extent of [[tirthas|tīrthas]]. Moreover, a number of [[tirthas|tīrthas]] scattered in different parts of India bear the same name (e. g. vide under [[Agnitirtha|Agnitīrtha]], [[Koțitirtha|Koṭitīrtha]], Cakratīrtha, [[Varāhatirtha|Varāhatīrtha]], [[Somatirtha|Somatīrtha]]). I am under great obligations to Cunningham’s ‘Ancient Geography of India’ [[(ed, of 1872)|(ed. of 1872)]] and to Nundo Lal Dey’s ‘The Geographical Dictionary of Ancient and Medieval India’ (1927). I have had occasions to differ from both, particularly from the latter. But, the space at my disposal being very limited, I could not enter into even brief discussions
